Read the left panel first. The more defenders in the box, the worse runs do: on these downs, designed runs averaged
about −0.03 EPA against five or fewer in the box, −0.05 against six, −0.09 against seven and −0.15 against eight or
more, and their success rates fell from about 41% to 34% across the same range.[^boxepa] Both data sources agree on
the slope. The plus-one is real: each defender the defense adds to the box takes something away from the run.

Now the right panel, which is the part that explains the two-high era. The same extra defender *helps the passing
game*. Dropbacks against five or fewer in the box averaged about +0.06 EPA; against seven, about +0.12; against eight or
more, about +0.16 in the 2018–2022 data. The box is a budget: a defender spent near the line is a defender not spent in
coverage, and the offense's passing game cashes the difference. (The 2023–2025 point for eight or more dropbacks rests on
only about 800 plays, which is why its interval is so wide.)

And look at the two panels side by side. **Against every box count, the average dropback beats the average designed
run.** Even against the lightest boxes, runs averaged less than zero EPA; even against the heaviest, dropbacks averaged
more than zero. The slopes are about the same size, too: an extra defender in the box takes roughly as much from the
run as it gives to the pass. So, on averages alone, the light box is close to a wash. Why call it a reasonable bet,
then? Three numbers from the same data tip it.

- **Where the big plays come from.** Against six in the box, 8% of dropbacks gained 20 yards or more; against seven, 11%.
  The share of designed runs gaining 10 or more barely moved: 12% against six, 12% against seven.[^explosive] Taking a
  safety out of the deep field buys the offense explosive passes; putting him back buys the run game almost nothing
  big. A defense that fears the long ball more than the four-yard run, as Fangio's does, is reading this line.
- **The run it gives up is still a losing play.** At −0.05 EPA, a designed run against a six-man box still leaves the
  offense slightly worse off, on average, than before the snap. Conceding it costs less than it looks on a rushing-yards
  table.
- **Don't expect the offense to be "steered."** You might think a light box lures offenses into running more. In
  these situations the raw numbers say the opposite: offenses ran on 43% of plays against six in the box and 55%
  against seven (same footnote). That is the defense's choice showing through, not the offense's: defenses lighten the box
  against spread formations that usually throw and load it against heavy ones that usually run. The bet is not that
  the offense will take the bait. It is that whatever the offense does, the defense has spent its players where the
  bigger danger is.

If dropbacks beat runs at every box count, why does anyone run? Because the averages only hold at the mix offenses
actually use. Runs keep defenses from dropping everyone into coverage; an offense that stopped running would soon see
those same dropbacks against eight defenders in coverage, and the gap would close. And this chart leaves out the
situations where running is clearly right: short yardage, the goal line, protecting a lead late. The light box is a
bet on the margin, not a claim that the run is dead.

Three cautions keep this honest.

- **The box count is measured at the snap.** A safety who rotates down after the snap, like the one in @fig-plus-one,
  is counted *out* of the box. Some "six-man boxes" in the data were seven-man fits a second later, which makes light
  boxes look a little better against the run than the fits really were.
- **Boxes are chosen, not assigned at random.** Defenses load the box when they expect a run and empty it when they
  expect a pass, and offenses check into runs against light boxes. Holding the down and the game situation fixed, as this
  chart does, removes the worst of that, but not all of it. [A First Look at
  Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) showed how flat these comparisons look
  when you don't.
- **The data changes source between 2022 and 2023.** Next Gen Stats (the NFL's player-tracking data) supplied the box
  count through 2022, and [FTN](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-ftn-charting-data), a data company whose staff chart
  every play by hand, from 2023. They draw the box differently, so read the two lines as two measurements, not one
  trend.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**Finding the force in tracking data.** The "Watch for it" rule (the outermost defender within about seven yards of
the line on each side, ignoring a corner who is deep or pressed on his man, but counting a corner who squats at about
five yards when both safeties are deep) is easy to turn into code. Here it is run on two simulated plays exported in
Big Data Bowl format (these frames are simulated, BDB-format, not real tracking): the single-high fit chart of
@fig-fit-chart and the two-high picture of Drill 1, below.

::: {#7555f65c .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (find the probable force player on each side at the snap)"}
ROLE = {"WE": "backside end (5)", "SE": "play-side end (5)", "SAM": "Sam (S)", "SS": "strong safety",
        "FS": "free safety", "LCB": "left corner", "RCB": "right corner", "NB": "nickel ($)",
        "MIKE": "Mike", "WILL": "Will", "NT": "nose (1)", "DT": "tackle (3)"}


def force_candidates(trk, max_depth=7.0, corner_depth=(3.0, 6.0), deep=10.0):
    """Outermost defender on each side within `max_depth` yards of the line at the snap: the probable force.
    A corner counts only if he squats `corner_depth` yards off the ball AND at least two defenders are deeper
    than `deep` (the Cover 2 'cloud' corner); a deep or pressed corner is ignored. A pre-snap guess:
    rotation after the snap can change it."""
    snap = trk[trk["frameType"] == "SNAP"]
    ball = snap[snap["side"] == "ball"].iloc[0]
    los, mid = ball["x"], ball["y"]
    dfn_all = snap[snap["side"] == "def"].copy()
    dfn_all["depth"] = dfn_all["x"] - los
    two_deep = (dfn_all["depth"] > deep).sum() >= 2
    rows = []
    for side_name, sgn in (("offense's right", -1), ("offense's left", 1)):   # offense faces +x: right = -y
        dfn = dfn_all[(dfn_all["y"] - mid) * sgn > 0].copy()
        dfn["width"] = (dfn["y"] - mid) * sgn
        corner = dfn["position"] == "CB"
        squat = corner & dfn["depth"].between(*corner_depth) & two_deep
        dfn = dfn[(dfn["depth"] <= max_depth) & (~corner | squat)]
        top = dfn.sort_values("width").iloc[-1]
        rows.append({"side": side_name, "probable force": ROLE.get(top["displayName"], top["displayName"]),
                     "yards outside the ball": round(top["width"], 1), "depth": round(top["depth"], 1)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


fit_play = Play(i_form(), sky_defense(), los=35, to_go=None)
cloud_play = Play(single_back_11(), even4() + [
    D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -6.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 4.5, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 4.5, 15.8, "CB"),
    D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -7.5, "FS")], los=35, to_go=None)
for name, play in [("Single-high fit chart (Cover 3, sky)", fit_play), ("Drill 1 (two-high, squatting corners)",
                                                                           cloud_play)]:
    print(name)
    print(force_candidates(play.to_tracking()).to_string(index=False), "\n")
```

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seattle Seahawks 2012–2015 (the eighth man)"}
The plus-one's most famous modern home was Pete Carroll's Seattle defense, built on single-high
[Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd). Earl Thomas played the deep middle, alone, and Kam
Chancellor, a strong safety built like a linebacker, played near the line as the eighth man in the box. Seattle led the
NFL in scoring defense four years running, 2012 through 2015.[^seattle] Watch any of their games from those seasons for
one thing: where Chancellor is at the snap. He is the force on runs to his side, the plus-one in the box count, and the
reason offenses that wanted to run on Seattle needed an extra blocker. Then watch what happens to Thomas when the
offense fakes the run: he is the only deep defender, which is the cost of the eighth man.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024 (the light box that held)"}
Vic Fangio's first Eagles defense, in 2024, is the light-box argument at full strength, and it started badly. Through the
first two weeks the *Philadelphia Inquirer* reported six or fewer defenders in the box on 73.5% of snaps, the
third-highest rate in the league, and the run defense looked shaky after the Falcons ran through it in Week 2.[^inq2]
Fangio kept the shape. Over the full season, by this book's count, opponents' designed runs met six or fewer in the box
about two thirds of the time (a different measure from the *Inquirer*'s early snap count, and again the third-highest
rate), and the Eagles allowed the fewest EPA per designed run in the league.[^fangiocalc] Every defense Fangio has run
since 2019 (he spent 2022 as a consultant) has been among the five that met runs with six or fewer in the box most
often.[^fangiocalc2] The bet rested on the interior of the line: tackles Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis, whom Fangio
called "a better run defender than he is a pass rusher," and Milton Williams.[^dtackles] What to watch: the two
safeties at 12–14 yards at the snap, the six-man box, and how often an interior lineman ends up with two blockers on him
and doesn't move. The defense is betting on the front, and in 2024 the bet paid off on the way to a Super Bowl LIX win
over Kansas City, 40–22.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2019 (the box that wasn't loaded enough)"}
The 2019 Ravens rushed for 3,296 yards, breaking an NFL team record that had stood since 1978, and Lamar Jackson ran for
1,206 of them on his way to a unanimous MVP.[^ravens] Box math explains why defenses could not simply load up. On a
designed run with Jackson reading a defender, every box needed one more defender than it appeared to, because the
quarterback counts as a blocker, and on a designed quarterback run (Jackson had 120 of them), the running back could
turn into one more lead blocker. Defenses met the Ravens' designed runs with seven or more in the box about 65% of the
time, slightly more than they did the rest of the league, and still lost: the Ravens averaged about +0.10 EPA per
designed run against seven-man boxes and about +0.04 against eight or more, where the league averaged −0.10 and −0.13.
Jackson's own designed runs averaged about 7.1 yards.[^ravenscalc] What looks like a normal seven-man box on the
broadcast was, against Baltimore, a light one. Watch any 2019 Ravens game for the defender the quarterback is reading,
and count him out of the box.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024 offense (running at two-high)"}
The same season, on the other side of the ball, the Eagles showed what a good run game does to a light box, with
a quarterback, Jalen Hurts, whom defenses also had to account for as a runner. Saquon Barkley ran for 2,005 yards, the ninth 2,000-yard season in NFL history.[^barkley] Against Philadelphia,
defenses played six or fewer in the box on about 61% of designed runs (the league rate was about 59%), and the Eagles
averaged about 5.4 yards per designed run against those boxes, against the league's 4.7. About one in seven of those
runs gained ten yards or more.[^eaglescalc] That is the light box's bill, paid in full: when the front cannot hold six
blockers and the safeties arrive at five yards instead of three, the runs that get past them go a long way. What to
watch: the safeties' depth at the snap, the double teams on the interior, and the moment Barkley reaches the second level
one-on-one with a safety coming downhill.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Before the snap**

- **Count the box, then count the blockers.** Five linemen, plus every tight end and fullback near the line. If the
  quarterback is a runner who reads a defender, add him. More defenders than blockers: the defense has its plus-one in
  the box. Even: the plus-one is a safety, and he will arrive late.
- **Find the force on each side.** Look for the outermost defender within about seven yards of the line. Ignore a
  corner who is deep or pressed on his receiver, but count a corner squatting at about five yards when both safeties
  are deep. A safety walked down outside the tight end: safety force (likely Cover 3, sky). Corners squatting at five
  yards with both safeties deep: corner force (likely Cover 2, cloud). A nickel or linebacker over the slot: he is the
  force on that side. Nobody out there but the end: the end is the force. With two tight ends or an unbalanced line,
  do it side by side: each side has its own end man and its own force.
- **Check the safeties' depth.** At 12–14 yards, they are alley players from depth and the box is what you see. At 8–10
  yards and creeping, one of them is probably coming down at the snap.

**After the snap**

- **Did a safety rotate down?** That is the plus-one arriving.
- **Watch the end man meet the kick-out or the puller.** Dives under it: spill, so look outside for the force. Stays
  square, outside arm free: box, so look inside for the linebacker filling.
- **Did the run bounce?** If it did, who met it outside, the force or nobody? If nobody, rewind and find the empty gap.
- **On a cutback, find the backside linebacker.** If he flowed with everyone else, that is the gap the runner used.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. Who's the force?** First-and-10, 11 personnel. The offense is about to run outside, to its right, toward
the tight end and the Z receiver. Before the snap the defense shows the picture below. Who is the force on the play
side, who is the alley player, and where do you expect the run to end up?

::: {#cell-fig-drill-1 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = single_back_11()
dfn = even4() + [D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -6.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 4.5, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 4.5, 15.8, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -7.5, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: who forces a run to the right?")
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-8.5, 15.0))
dashed(f, p, [(-7.0, 0.0), (-5.6, 4.0), (-2.6, 8.5), (0.4, 11.0)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.4)
say(f, p, -4.6, 11.8, "the run is\nheaded here", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 1: before the snap. Both safeties are deep, 12 yards off the ball and about 7 or 8 yards either side of it, a little outside the hash marks (not drawn); both corners are squatting at about 5 yards, a step outside their receivers, facing the quarterback; six defenders in the box against six blockers.](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math_files/figure-html/fig-drill-1-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-1}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The right cornerback is the force; the strong safety is the alley player.** Two deep safeties and two corners
squatting at five yards, outside their receivers, with their eyes on the quarterback is the classic Cover 2 shape. The corners have no deep zone
to protect, so the play-side corner is free to come up outside-in, keep the ball inside him and turn it back. The
strong safety, starting at twelve yards, reads run and comes down into the alley between the corner and the box.

Expect the run to be turned back inside around the numbers, and expect the defense to *give up some yards* doing it:
six in the box against six blockers is a light box, and the alley player is arriving from twelve yards. The offense's
best counter is a receiver blocking the corner (the Z cracking down, or simply blocking him out), which is why, against
Cover 2, the wide receivers' blocks matter so much in the run game. One caution: corners squatting at five yards can also
be a disguise, bailing to deep thirds at the snap
([Disguise and Rotation](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)). If that happens, the force
becomes whoever rotates down, usually a safety.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. Do the box math.** Second-and-6. The offense is in shotgun with 11 personnel, and its quarterback is one of
the league's most dangerous runners. The defense shows two high safeties and six defenders in the box. How many
blockers does the offense really have, who is the defense's free man, and what run do you expect?

::: {#cell-fig-drill-2 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = single_back_11(gun=True)
dfn = even4() + [D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -6.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.5, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=6, title="Drill 2: count the box, then count the blockers")
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-8.0, 15.0))
lane(f, p, -5.4, 7.6, -0.6, 7.0, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.05)
say(f, p, 9.2, 0.0, "the box", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 2: before the snap. Shotgun, one back beside the quarterback, a tight end on the right; four defensive linemen and two linebackers in the box, a nickel back outside it on the left, two safeties at 12 to 13 yards.](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math_files/figure-html/fig-drill-2-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-2}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Seven blockers against six, and the deep free men are twelve yards away.** Five linemen and the tight end make six
blockers, and the box holds six defenders: even. But a quarterback who runs and reads counts as a blocker, because the
defender he reads is "blocked" by the read. So on a zone read the offense is effectively seven against six, plus-one *in
the offense's favour*. The defense's free men are the two safeties.

One more defender belongs in the count: the nickel back ($), the
[overhang defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-overhang-defender) outside the box on the left. With the back
beside the quarterback on the left, the zone read's keep goes left, straight at him, so on the keep side he can play
the quarterback and the math there is really seven against seven. That is why offenses pair the read with a quick
throw to the slot receiver (a bubble or a glance, the [RPO](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) idea): if the $
comes down to take the quarterback, the throw goes behind him, and the slot "blocks" him without touching him.

Expect a zone read, or a run with the quarterback as a threat, likely with that throw attached, and expect it to gain
four or five yards before a safety arrives, unless the defense has a plan. Its plans: rotate a safety down at the snap
(watch for one creeping toward 8–9 yards before the ball is snapped), or exchange gaps on the read man (the end
crashes, a linebacker scrapes to the quarterback, @fig-exchange). If the safeties stay deep and the end sits still,
this is the picture the 2019 Ravens punished whenever they got it, and it is a good one for the offense.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. The force is the target.** First-and-10. The offense is in the I-formation and the defense is in a
single-high shell, a 4-3 Over with the Sam walked up on the line and the strong safety down outside him, the shape of
@fig-fit-chart. One thing is
different: the Z receiver has lined up much closer to the formation than usual. What is the offense planning, and who
on the defense has to be ready?

::: {#cell-fig-drill-3 .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = [q.moved(w=9.0) if q.key == "Z" else q for q in i_form()]
dfn = over_front() + [D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS"),
                      D("LCB", "CB", 7.5, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 11.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 3: why is the Z so close?")
p.highlight("Z", color=BALL_RING); p.highlight("SAM", color=WATCH_RING)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
point_to(f, p, (-4.8, 13.2), (-1.5, 9.0), "tight split", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 3: before the snap. 21 personnel in the I-formation; a 4-3 Over with the Sam walked up on the line (orange ring), the strong safety down at about 6 yards outside the tight end and one deep safety. The Z receiver is in a tight split, about 9 yards from the ball instead of out near the numbers.](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math_files/figure-html/fig-drill-3-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-3}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A crack block on the force, so the cornerback must replace him.** The defense's fit against power depends on the
strong safety: he is the force, the man outside the spill. A receiver in a tight split is in perfect position to block
*down* on him at the snap, a [crack block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-block)
([Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd)), from the side, where
the safety is not looking. If the defense spills the kick-out and the force has been cracked, the bounce has nobody
outside it.

So the defender who must be ready is the right cornerback. His rule is *crack-replace*: when the receiver in front of
him blocks in, he stops thinking about his deep third and comes up to become the force himself. Many defenses tie this
to the split before the snap: a reduced split triggers a "crack!" call, so the corner and the safety both know the
crack-replace is on, and some staffs also switch the end man from spill to box so the ball stays inside. A tight split
is also the classic tell for [crack-toss](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-toss), where the ball goes straight
to the edge the crack has cleared. Watch the corner's first step after the snap. If it is forward and outside, the defense saw the crack coming. If it is backward, the run is
going to the sideline.
:::
:::

## Back to the replay

Return to the opening play. The offense ran power to the right; the end man threw himself under the fullback; the back
bounced outside and was tackled by a safety who started twelve yards deep. Now you can name every piece of it. The end man
was the **spill** player, and the pile he made was the point: the pulling guard had no lane, and the ball went sideways.
The safety who made the tackle was either the **force** (if he had come down to the edge) or the **alley player** (if
he filled the lane inside the force from depth), and he had been free all along, the defense's **plus-one**, never
assigned to any blocker. The analyst said "great fit" because every defender between the ball and the sideline did his
job and nobody did anyone else's. Nobody beat a block. The arithmetic did the work.

## Takeaways

- **A run fit is an eleven-man plan.** Every gap has exactly one owner (gap integrity), and every owner knows how his
  gap moves when the blocking changes. Two defenders in one gap means an empty gap somewhere else.
- **Force turns the ball back inside.** The force defender is a role, not a position: the end, a linebacker, a safety
  or a corner, depending on the call. The coverage usually decides who is free to be him (safety force in Cover 3,
  corner force in Cover 2).
- **Spill and box send the ball to opposite places.** Spill wrong-arms the kick-out and bounces the ball outside to
  speed (and dares the offense to log it); box keeps the outside arm free and squeezes the ball inside to the
  linebackers. Each is a promise about who is waiting, and the alley player fills the lane between the box and the
  force, coming inside-out as the force comes outside-in.
- **The plus-one is the extra defender, and it usually comes from a safety.** Offenses erase it with an extra blocker,
  a quarterback read or a pass; defenses get it back with rotation, gap exchanges or two-gapping fronts. Count the
  quarterback when he runs.
- **The light box is a bet, not a mistake.** Two-high defenses give up a few yards per carry, four or five before the
  safeties arrive, to protect against the explosive pass. In 2018–2025 data, each extra box defender cost runs about as
  much on average as it gave passes, but it bought the passing game far more big plays than it took from the run game,
  and the run the light box concedes still averages below zero EPA.
